title: Prefix key entropy & TTL safety playbook for KV cache cost tuning
creator: Marina Patel
description:
Summary:
This ticket captures a practical playbook for improving cache unit economics by (1) modeling realistic hit-rate under varying prefix/key designs, (2) defining TTL and eviction policy tuning heuristics that are safe to roll out automatically, and (3) standardizing cache key normalization to reduce low-value cardinality. The goal is a deterministic, auditable autotuner that proposes conservative config changes and a safe rollback circuit if user-visible latency or error SLOs regress.

Background and motivation:
- We see uneven cache value across customers and routes: some prefixes are extremely hot and safe to cache aggressively, while others are high-cardinality and impose high memory costs with minimal hit benefit.
- Current manual tuning is slow and brittle; we want an automation surface (recommendations + opt-in apply) that reduces per-token cost by 10-30% on targeted workloads without increasing tail latency.

What this doc covers (deliverables):
1) Offline hit-rate estimator: workload sampler + Monte Carlo estimator that simulates TTL & bucketization trade-offs for a route or prefix.
2) Key design guidance: normalization rules, entropy bucketing heuristic, and collision avoidance for user-generated tokens.
3) TTL policy family and safety heuristics: warm-start TTLs, decay schedules, and rollback triggers tied to SLOs and token cost.
4) Rollout plan and safety circuits: canary %, metric thresholds, automated rollback criteria, and human-in-the-loop stalls.
5) Dashboard & alerts: metrics to show before/after cost, hit-rate, tail latency, and memory pressure.

Technical approach - hit-rate modeling:
- Input data: request logs with normalized key prefixes, timestamp, sequence length, route, and model variant. We sample using stratified sampling (by route and peak QPS window) to preserve tail behavior.
- Estimator: run a Monte Carlo simulation of request arrival ordering (preserving original timestamps), apply candidate TTL/ejection policies, and compute hit-rate, average memory footprint, and per-token cost delta. Include KV-cache warmup and cold-start windows.
- Uncertainty quantification: run multiple resamples and produce a 90% confidence interval on hit-rate and cost delta. Report both mean and P10/P90 cost outcomes so ops can understand downside risk.
- Synthetic workload generator: when logs are insufficient (cold route), use a parameterized generator (zipfian key popularity, temporal locality factor) to produce candidates for simulation.

Key design & normalization rules (guidelines):
- Canonicalization: remove ephemeral query params, lower-case host/service names, and canonicalize timestamps to minute buckets for non-identity keys.
- Entropy bucketing: compute per-key entropy score (hash-based rolling sample). If entropy < threshold A -> treat as stable prefix and allow longer TTL; if entropy > threshold B -> prefer small TTL / no-cache or coarse-grained prefixing.
- Prefix shaping: allow two-layer keys: (stable-prefix)::::(shard-id)::::(user-entropy). Default recommendations: for stable-prefixes, use prefix-level cache; for user-entropy heavy keys, trim to first N characters or hash and use low-resolution bucket.
- Collision mitigation: when hashing/trimming, include namespace and model-variant in digest; detect sudden growth in collision count in telemetry and revert to safer policy.

TTL & policy tuning heuristics:
- Warm-start TTL: start with a modest TTL (e.g., 60s) for previously untested prefixes and monitor hit-rate delta over a 1-hour canary.
- Growth schedule: if hit-rate improves and memory pressure is low, grow TTL multiplicatively (60s -> 300s -> 900s) with checkpoints at each step.
- Aggressive candidates: candidates with stable hot-tail (P95 request repeat within TTL window > 0.7) can be suggested for immediate extension by an operator.
- Eviction policy: LRU with segregated hot-list for stable prefixes; for very large keys, use size-aware eviction to avoid single huge values causing churn.

Autotune safety & rollback rules:
- Success criteria to continue rollout: no >5% increase in P99 latency and no >2x increase in 5xx rate for the affected route. Cost reduction must be non-negative (we require projected cost savings) to progress to wider rollout.
- Stop & rollback triggers: sustained latency regressions beyond threshold for 5 minutes, memory oversubscription events, or a negative lower-bound on cost savings in the 90% CI.
- Circuit breaker: if any downstream failure (e.g., model-serving OOMs or GC spikes) is correlated (correlation coefficient > 0.6) with rollout time windows, immediately revert to previous stable policy and open a PagerDuty incident.

Rollout plan (canary -> staged -> full):
1) Local simulation and offline review: generate recommendation + estimator report.
2) Small canary (1-3% traffic on a single region/route) for 30 minutes with high-frequency sampling (10s) of metrics.
3) Expand to 10% for 2 hours if canary passes.
4) Gradual ramp to 50% then 100% over multiple cycles if metrics remain stable.

Telemetry and dashboards (minimum):
- route/prefix hit-rate (mean & CI), memory footprint, TTL distribution, P50/P95/P99 latency, 5xx rate, collision rate metric, and cost-per-token delta.
- Visualize estimator confidence bands versus observed.

Acceptance criteria (how we know this is done):
- The offline estimator runs on historical logs and produces reproducible hit-rate and cost profiles for 90% of tested routes.
- A working canary pipeline exists that can apply suggestions to a single route and automatically roll back on threshold breaches.
- A clear set of key-normalization rules and entropy-bucketing code is checked into the runtime repo with unit tests and a Confluence design doc.
- Dashboards with defined alert thresholds are available in the Console within the release window.

Operational notes and trade-offs:
- Over-aggressive bucketization reduces memory but may increase miss-rate and therefore model calls — tuning must prioritize tail latency SLOs over cost for customer-facing routes.
- Synthetic generators can misestimate real user behavior; always validate on a small canary before scaling.
- For routes with PII in keys, ensure normalization and hashing complies with KMS/HSM policies; mark such prefixes as "do not store" if required.

Next steps / action items:
- Build Monte Carlo estimator prototype and run against 7 days of logs for top 50 routes (owner: Liam).
- Implement entropy-bucketing library and unit tests (owner: Eng SDK team).
- Wire a canary pipeline that can apply TTL proposals via feature flag and revert automatically (owner: Infra SRE).
- Author Confluence playbook and run a postmortem checklist after the first rollout (owner: PM).
